Procurement & compliance · Tanzania

Working with AfriScan in Tanzania: procurement, local content and data

Tanzanian buyers of mapping and survey work apply three sets of rules on top of the technical scope. The Public Procurement Act, 2023 governs public tenders, the Petroleum Act and the Mining (Local Content) Regulations govern oil, gas and mining contracts, and the Personal Data Protection Act governs any personal data. These notes set out what applies to this kind of service, as of 27 September 2026, and what to ask any supplier for. They are not legal advice.

Request a proposal Send tender documents

How an engagement runs

From your route file to a reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route, wayleave or site file, the regions it crosses, the widths from your own licence or agreement, and what the record is for. We reply with the questions we need answered.

  2. Proposal

    A written proposal with the scope, the imagery plan and its dates, the method, the deliverables and the schedule. It names the contracting company, its local-content position, where data are stored, and, for any drone element, the company that will fly and the approvals its flights need.

  3. Survey and review

    Satellite screening of the whole area, drone detail where it earns its place, and a person reviewing every result before it reaches you.

  4. Delivery

    A PDF report in English and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers, sent only to the contacts you name.

Every project starts with scoping your route or site. How we work in general, and the engagement models we offer, are on how we work.

Public tenders

The Public Procurement Act, 2023

Act No. 10 of 2023, English version GN 813 of 20 September 2024. Public procuring entities, state utilities among them, run their procurement through NeST, the National e-Procurement System of Tanzania.

Section What it says
s.53(3) A foreign tenderer selected as lowest evaluated or best ranked must register with the appropriate professional statutory body and prove registration as an approved supplier, contractor or consultant
s.56 A margin of preference for Tanzanian goods, contractors and consultants: Tanzania-incorporated, with the majority of paid-up share capital owned by the Government or citizens
s.57 Where a Tanzanian public body funds the procurement, contracts below regulatory thresholds are reserved for local persons or firms
s.58 Foreign firms in non-emergency consultancies must include local firms and experts: up to 15 per cent of the score for local firms, and up to 10 per cent for national experts
s.61 Procuring entities set aside part of their annual volume for local individuals and firms; in a capacity-building joint venture with a foreign firm, “the local firm shall be the leading firm”
s.62 Above a threshold, foreign tenderers for works and non-consultancy services form joint ventures with, or subcontract, local firms at a prescribed percentage, and attach the agreement to the tender
s.63 Local firms under ss.58 and 61 must have share capital “wholly owned by citizens”
s.64 Set-asides for special groups: women, youth, the elderly and persons with special needs
s.66 Tender documents are in Kiswahili or English
s.73 Procurement is “implemented and reported through the electronic public procurement system”, which PPRA runs as NeST

Source: the Public Procurement Act, 2023, on the PPRA website. Whether mapping from imagery is procured as a consultancy or a non-consultancy service, and which thresholds apply, is for your procurement team to decide under the Act and its regulations.

Oil, gas and mining

The local-content rules for this kind of service

Petroleum

Under the Petroleum Act, Cap. 392, s.219, licence holders, contractors and subcontractors “shall give preference to goods which are produced or available in Tanzania and services which are rendered by Tanzanian citizens or local companies”. Goods and services not available locally are supplied by a company in a joint venture with a local company holding at least 25 per cent, or as the regulations provide. A “local company” is wholly owned by Tanzanian citizens, or is in a joint venture or partnership with citizens holding at least 15 per cent (s.219(9)). Licence holders file a procurement plan of at least five years with PURA (s.219(4)), and PURA runs a common qualification system for upstream suppliers.

Pipeline wayleaves in Tanzania

Mining

Under the Mining (Local Content) Regulations, 2018, as amended, an indigenous Tanzanian company has at least 20 per cent citizen equity and Tanzanians in at least 80 per cent of executive and senior management posts and all other posts. A non-indigenous company supplying a contractor, a subcontractor or a licensee must form a joint venture giving an indigenous Tanzanian company at least 20 per cent of the equity (reg 8(6)), and larger contracts are notified to the Mining Commission (reg 16). Each mining proposal sets out how it meets reg 8(6): the indigenous Tanzanian company and its equity share. Check the current text with the Mining Commission.

Mining in Tanzania

Personal data

The Personal Data Protection Act, Cap. 44

English version GN 395B of 13 June 2023. Personal data are taarifa binafsi, and the regulator is the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC, Tume ya Ulinzi wa Taarifa Binafsi). It applies in Mainland Tanzania and Tanzania Zanzibar, except for non-Union matters in Zanzibar.

  • Registration first. “A person shall not collect or process personal data without being registered as a data controller or a data processor under this Act” (s.14(1)). Private organisations register online with a BRELA certificate, a TIN certificate and an audited financial report, and introduce their Data Protection Officer by letter (PDPC registration).
  • Security. Controllers and processors keep personal data secure (s.27).
  • Transfers outside Tanzania. To states with adequate protection (s.31), or otherwise under s.32; the PDPC issues cross-border transfer permits.
  • Enforcement. Enforcement and penalty notices (ss.45–46) and administrative fines (s.47), with offences for unlawful disclosure (s.60) and for unlawful destruction or alteration of personal data (s.61).
  • Inspections. On 28 August 2026 the PDPC began compliance inspections of data controllers and processors, covering registration, the Data Protection Officer’s duties, how data are collected and stored, transfers under ss.31–32 and security under s.27(1).

What counts as personal data here

Building footprints on their own are generally not personal data, in our reading. Drone frames that show identifiable people, lists of project-affected persons and household data are. Our registers describe structures and carry no names, so the PAP list and the census stay with your team, and each contract says who processes what and where.

Drone approvals

Who flies, and what they need

Under the Civil Aviation (Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems) Regulations, 2026 (GN 268 of 2026), commercial drone work needs an RPAS Operator Certificate, which TCAA issues only to an applicant with a principal place of business registered in Tanzania, a security clearance and an approved security programme. Each operation needs TCAA’s authorisation, and a Category B risk assessment goes in at least 14 days ahead.

Drone surveys are subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires. Afridrone is working towards Tanzanian drone approvals, and every drone proposal names the company that will fly, with its ROC, operations specifications and the approvals its flights rely on.

Drone law in Tanzania

Where we work

Satellite everywhere, field and drone work where it is safe and approved

Satellite mapping covers the whole of Tanzania with no one on site. Field and drone work is planned job by job, against the approvals each job needs and current government travel advice.

Where current travel advice is against travel to an area, our work there is satellite-only, and we check that advice again when each job is planned. Military sites, State House, prisons and other protected places are left out of every deliverable.

Scope, stated plainly

  • Satellite work: the whole country, remotely
  • Field and drone work: planned per job against current travel advice; satellite-only where it advises against travel
  • Law notes: Mainland Tanzania; Zanzibar has its own land laws and is scoped separately
  • Reports: English

For procurement teams

What to ask any supplier, including us

Ask for these in the proposal. Where a supplier cannot show one, the proposal should say so and how it will be met.

  1. The contracting company

    Its name, where it is registered and its principal place of business; for work inside Tanzania, the BRELA certificate and TIN of the Tanzanian company involved.

  2. Local-content position

    For petroleum work, how the contract meets the Petroleum Act, s.219; for mining, the indigenous Tanzanian company and its equity share under reg 8(6); for public tenders, the local inclusion the Public Procurement Act, 2023 scores.

  3. Registrations for your tender

    NeST registration for public tenders, and registration with the professional statutory body after award where s.53(3) applies.

  4. Personal data

    The PDPC registration of whoever processes personal data, its Data Protection Officer, where the data are stored, the retention period and the basis for any transfer outside Tanzania (ss.31–32).

  5. Drone approvals

    The company that will fly, its ROC and operations specifications, security clearance, registered drones, pilots with Tanzanian remote pilot licences and insurance, as the drone-law checklist sets out.

  6. Imagery

    Which imagery the deliverables rest on and its capture dates; map-service basemaps are never the dated record.

  7. Review and limits

    Who reviews results before delivery, and what the survey cannot show: people, underground works, leaks or anything under optical cloud.

Frequently asked questions

Can a foreign firm be awarded a Tanzanian public tender?

Yes, subject to the Public Procurement Act, 2023. A foreign tenderer selected as the lowest evaluated or best ranked must then register with the appropriate professional statutory body and prove its registration as an approved supplier, contractor or consultant (s.53(3)). Foreign consultancy bids are scored on the inclusion of local firms and experts (s.58), and above a threshold, foreign tenderers for works and non-consultancy services must form a joint venture with, or subcontract, local firms (s.62).

Which company will contract with us?

Each proposal names the contracting company, where it is registered and its local-content position for your contract. For mining work, it sets out how the contract meets reg 8(6) of the Mining (Local Content) Regulations, naming the indigenous Tanzanian company and its equity share. For petroleum work, it shows how the contract meets the Petroleum Act, s.219.

Where will our data be processed and stored?

The proposal says so, together with the retention period and how any transfer of personal data outside Tanzania is covered under the Personal Data Protection Act, ss.31–32. Our registers describe structures and carry no names; lists of project-affected persons stay with your team or your RAP consultant.

Can tender documents be in Kiswahili?

Yes. Under the Public Procurement Act, 2023, tender documents are in Kiswahili or English (s.66). Our reports and GIS layers are in English.

Do you work everywhere in Tanzania?

Satellite work covers the whole country, with no one on site. Field and drone work is planned job by job against the approvals each job needs and current government travel advice; where that advice is against travel to an area, our work there is satellite-only. Our law notes cover Mainland Tanzania; Zanzibar has its own land laws, so work there is scoped separately.

Send your RFQ or tender with the route

Name the tender or RFQ number and the portal, attach any prequalification or vendor forms, and send the route or site file. We reply with the questions we need answered and a written proposal that names the contracting company and its local-content position.
